Volume 07 · Chapter 01

Transactions and double-entry accounting

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v01

By the endRecord transactions and preserve the accounting equation.

Capability and prerequisites

After this chapter, you can turn a documented business event into a balanced journal entry, post it to accounts, adjust for timing, and reconcile the resulting assets, liabilities and equity. You can also explain why a perfectly balanced ledger can contain a serious accounting error. Read Volume 1, especially stocks, flows and balance sheets. No prior bookkeeping vocabulary is assumed.

A bank receipt says that cash increased. It does not tell you whether the company borrowed, sold a service, collected an old bill or received an owner's contribution. Those events have different obligations and different effects on profit. Double entry records the linked consequences; recognition and measurement determine which consequences belong in the books and at what amount.

1. Define the entity, period and rules first

Our reporting entity is Harbor Calibration Services, a fictional corporation separate from its owners. Its ledger uses US dollars, displayed below as whole dollars; the downloadable journal stores integer cents. The main period is January 2025, with zero opening balances. The company, documents and dates are entirely synthetic. The owner's private savings and household purchases are outside this reporting entity unless the company itself enters a transaction with the owner.

An asset represents a resource or right the entity controls now because of an earlier event, with potential economic benefit. Examples here are cash, a collectible customer bill and equipment available for use. A liability represents an existing obligation to provide resources: repayment to a lender, payment to employees or promised services for a customer advance. Equity is the residual claim measured as recorded assets less recorded liabilities. It can be negative. Book equity is not a promise of the amount owners could obtain by selling the company.

Assets = liabilities + equity.
Change in assets = change in liabilities + change in equity.

Recognition asks whether and when an item enters the accounts; measurement asks its monetary amount; classification asks which account describes it. A purchase order, a delivery, an invoice and a payment can occur on four different days. An invoice alone does not prove that a service was performed, and lack of an invoice does not prove that employees have not earned wages. Record the economic event and supporting evidence, not merely whichever document arrives first.

The IFRS Foundation's March 2018 Conceptual Framework project summary separates element definitions, recognition and measurement. It emphasizes useful, faithfully represented information and makes clear that the Framework is not itself an IFRS Standard and cannot override one. That dated conceptual reference is not a conclusion that this exercise satisfies any jurisdiction's reporting requirements. We use the following explicit teaching conventions; advanced contracts, uncertainty and applicable standards require further analysis.

  • Service revenue is recorded for the specified completed service when the customer owes the stated, fully collectible amount. An unconditional unpaid bill becomes a receivable. An advance for an unperformed session remains a liability until that session is delivered.
  • Supplies and prepaid insurance begin as assets; their specified consumption becomes expense. Equipment begins at purchase cost. With no impairment, disposal or revaluation, its stipulated depreciable cost is allocated evenly over its useful months, starting when available for use.
  • Wages become expense as employees perform the stated work. Interest accrues under the supplied monthly contract. An unpaid amount becomes a payable. Principal repayment reduces debt rather than expense.
  • Owner contributions increase contributed capital. An authorized dividend reduces owners' equity; it does not buy a service and is not an expense. Our dividend is declared and paid on the same day, so no intervening dividend payable is needed.
  • There are no taxes, foreign currencies, inventory sales, other comprehensive income, bad debts, leases, groups or changes of accounting policy. Cash cannot be negative unless a separate financing arrangement is supplied.

These exclusions keep the entries determinate. They do not mean that real firms may ignore the excluded items. Nor does “matching” permit inventing an asset to postpone an inconvenient expense. First establish the resource, obligation and applicable recognition rule; then record the timing consequences.

2. Accounts, debits and credits

An account collects movements of one defined kind, such as Cash or Wages payable. The chart of accounts lists the names and their classifications. A T-account displays additions to its left and right sides. Debit, abbreviated Dr, means the left side; credit, Cr, means the right. Neither word universally means increase, decrease, good, bad, cash received or debt incurred.

Normal balance and increase direction in our chart; Harbor, USD
Account classIncreaseDecreaseExamples
AssetsDebitCreditCash, receivables, supplies, prepaid insurance, equipment cost
LiabilitiesCreditDebitTrade payables, customer advances, wages/interest payable, loan principal
Contributed capital and retained earningsCreditDebitOwners' funding and accumulated retained results
RevenueCreditDebitService revenue; a temporary increase in equity
ExpensesDebitCreditWages, supplies, insurance, depreciation, interest
DistributionsDebitCreditDividends; a temporary reduction of equity
Contra assetCreditDebitAccumulated depreciation, deducted from equipment cost

A normal balance is the side on which a class ordinarily accumulates. It is not a theorem forbidding an opposite balance. Retained earnings can show a debit deficit after losses. A debit supplier-payable balance might indicate a supplier advance, an overpayment or an error and requires investigation and possibly reclassification. Accumulated depreciation normally has a credit balance but is not a liability: it offsets an asset, not an amount promised to a creditor.

For an asset account, a debit increases its recorded amount. For a loan liability, a credit increases the amount owed. Thus borrowing $500 is Dr Cash 500 and Cr Loan 500. Paying that principal is Dr Loan 500 and Cr Cash 500. A bank describing a deposit as a “credit” is speaking from its own liability ledger; the customer's deposit is an asset in the customer's books. Specify whose account you mean.

Kothari's MIT accounting-process notes provide the primary teaching route for ledger sides, temporary accounts and the journal-to-trial-balance sequence. The entries and business below are original; none of the course's worked businesses is reproduced.

Why the two sides must balance

Before closing, keep this month's revenue, expenses and dividends in separate temporary accounts, so readers can see how retained earnings changed. With no other equity changes in our model,

Equity at period end = contributed capital at period end + retained earnings at period start
+ current revenue − current expenses − current dividends.
Therefore: assets + expenses + dividends
= liabilities + contributed capital + opening retained earnings + revenue.

The asset total here already subtracts accumulated depreciation. Reserve the term net assets for assets minus liabilities, which equals equity. Debits increase the left-side classes, while credits increase the right-side classes; reductions use the opposite side. A journal entry has equal total debits and credits, though it can contain more than two lines. A transaction exchanging cash for equipment debits one asset and credits another. Revenue on credit debits an asset and credits revenue. Paying wages debits expense and credits an asset.

For a compact proof, give every account a signed ledger balance equal to cumulative debits minus cumulative credits, including its opening balance. A complete opening trial balance sums to zero. Every balanced entry adds zero to that sum. After any number of such entries the sum is still zero, because adding zero repeatedly preserves it. Grouping those signed balances by the specified account classes produces the expanded equation above. This proves an arithmetic invariant. It cannot prove that a recorded service happened, that a price is appropriate, or that the chart classified the item correctly.

3. From evidence to journal to ledger

The journal records entries in dated order with a source reference and explanation. Posting transfers each line to its account in the ledger. The trial balance lists the resulting account balances, with debit balances in one column and credit balances in the other. An account with both debit and credit movements contributes its net balance, not all its transactions, to the trial balance.

Use this sequence: identify the reporting entity and event date; decide what resource, obligation or owner claim changed; apply the stated recognition and measurement rule; name the affected accounts; choose their sides and amounts; then check total debits against credits. Keep the invoice, receipt, completion record or adjustment workpaper linked to the entry. The posting date can differ from the period to which an item belongs. In our example, January-end adjustments are prepared on 2 February but belong to January.

Worked example 1 — A complete January transaction journal

Harbor begins January with no assets, liabilities or equity. All numbers below are USD. Equipment is available on 1 January, costs 3,600, has zero residual value and has 36 equal months of expected use. Insurance bought on 1 January covers six equal months through June. The loan starts on 1 January and charges exactly 1% for January, payable later. Evidence establishes the supplied service and payroll facts. None of these estimates is inferred merely from a bank statement.

Harbor transaction journal before month-end adjustments, January 2025; USD
ID/date and evidenceDebitCreditReason
J01, 1 Jan: owner subscription and receiptCash 6,000Contributed capital 6,000Owner financing, not revenue
J02, 1 Jan: executed loanCash 2,400Loan principal 2,400Cash with a repayment obligation
J03, 1 Jan: equipment delivery/paymentEquipment cost 3,600Cash 3,600Exchange of assets
J04, 1 Jan: insurance policy/paymentPrepaid insurance 1,200Cash 1,200Right to future coverage
J05, 5 Jan: supplies received on invoiceSupplies 900Trade payables 900Received asset and amount owed
J06, 15 Jan: two completed service ordersCash 1,800; receivables 2,400Service revenue 4,200Compound entry: total debits 4,200
J07, 18 Jan: advance for four $250 sessionsCash 1,000Customer advances 1,000No session performed at receipt
J08, 22 Jan: collection against J06Cash 900Receivables 900Collection does not earn the service again
J09, 24 Jan: supplier payment against J05Trade payables 500Cash 500Settlement does not consume supplies again
J10, 28 Jan: wages earned and paidWages expense 1,100Cash 1,100January employee service consumed
J11, 29 Jan: authorized dividend paidDividends 400Cash 400Distribution to owners, not employee expense

Post the cash lines explicitly. Debits are 6,000 + 2,400 + 1,800 + 1,000 + 900 = 12,100. Credits are 3,600 + 1,200 + 500 + 1,100 + 400 = 6,800. The net debit Cash balance is 5,300. Receivables have debit 2,400 and credit 900, leaving debit 1,500. Trade payables have credit 900 and debit 500, leaving credit 400. These are three ledger accounts, not three new transactions.

The unadjusted debit balances are cash 5,300, receivables 1,500, supplies 900, prepaid insurance 1,200, equipment 3,600, wages expense 1,100 and dividends 400: total 14,000. Credits are trade payables 400, advances 1,000, loan 2,400, capital 6,000 and revenue 4,200: also 14,000. The provisional profit is 4,200 − 1,100 = 3,100. Equal columns do not make this a finished January result: supplies, coverage, asset use and unpaid labor have not yet been recognized, and part of the advance has since been earned.

4. Accruals and adjustments align the account with the period

Accrual accounting records the consequences of activity in its specified period even if cash moves earlier or later. An accrued expense recognizes consumed service before payment; an accrued revenue recognizes completed service before collection, possibly before billing. A deferral begins with cash but postpones the expense or revenue because coverage or performance remains in the future. These are timing categories, not judgments about whether cash matters.

Four timing patterns under our stated recognition rules
TimingInitial entryLater entry
Service before customer cashDr Receivables; Cr RevenueDr Cash; Cr Receivables
Customer cash before serviceDr Cash; Cr Customer advancesDr Customer advances; Cr Revenue as specified service is completed
Employee work before paymentDr Wages expense; Cr Wages payableDr Wages payable; Cr Cash for the accrued portion
Insurance cash before coverage expiresDr Prepaid insurance; Cr CashDr Insurance expense; Cr Prepaid insurance for consumed coverage

An adjusting entry brings a balance into line with the period-end evidence. Our accrual and cost-allocation adjustments contain no new cash payment. This does not imply that every correction prepared during a close must exclude Cash: an omitted bank charge, for example, can require a cash correction. Distinguish a timing adjustment from correcting an already recorded amount or adding a missing transaction.

Depreciation in this case allocates a stated cost; it is not a cash deposit into a replacement fund and does not measure each month's market-price change. With cost C, residual value S, N positive useful months and m full months of use, our straight-line convention gives monthly expense (C − S)/N, accumulated depreciation min{m,N}(C − S)/N, and carrying amount C minus accumulated depreciation. Require C ≥ S ≥ 0. Stop at the residual value; continued use does not automatically require a negative book value. Actual estimates, impairment and revisions require their own facts and rules.

The MIT notes on periodic adjustments distinguish prepaid resources, advances, unpaid expenses and cost allocation. We use the mechanics, while keeping this chapter's numerical rules explicit rather than treating dated teaching statements as current GAAP instructions.

Worked example 2 — Adjust, prove the balances and close the month

At 31 January, the count finds supplies costing 300. One insurance month expired. Equipment was available for the full month. Employees earned another 250, unpaid. Loan interest for January is 2,400 × 0.01 = 24, unpaid. A signed completion record shows one of the four $250 sessions was delivered by 31 January. Prepare these adjustments on 2 February, with January-effective dates:

Harbor adjustments effective 31 January 2025; USD

Supplies consumed: 900 − 300 = 600Supplies expense 600Supplies 600
Coverage consumed: 1,200/6 = 200Insurance expense 200Prepaid insurance 200
Equipment allocation: 3,600/36 = 100Depreciation expense 100Accumulated depreciation 100
Unpaid January work: 250Wages expense 250Wages payable 250
Unpaid January interest: 24Interest expense 24Interest payable 24
One prepaid session now completed: 250Customer advances 250Service revenue 250

The adjusted trial balance is:

Harbor adjusted trial balance, 31 January 2025; USD, before closing
AccountDebit balanceCredit balance
Cash5,3000
Trade receivables1,5000
Supplies3000
Prepaid insurance1,0000
Equipment at cost3,6000

Revenue is 4,450. Expenses are 1,350 + 600 + 200 + 100 + 24 = 2,274. January profit is therefore 2,176. The adjustment reduced provisional profit by 924: new expense 1,174 less new revenue 250. Cash remains 5,300 because none of these six adjustments changes it.

Total assets, after deducting accumulated depreciation, are 5,300 + 1,500 + 300 + 1,000 + 3,600 − 100 = 11,600. Liabilities are 400 + 750 + 250 + 24 + 2,400 = 3,824. Equity is 6,000 + 2,176 − 400 = 7,776. Thus 11,600 = 3,824 + 7,776. The $14,374 trial-balance total is not assets or company value: it also contains temporary expense and dividend balances, and presents the contra asset on the credit side.

Closing entries transfer temporary balances to retained earnings after preserving the month's performance information. Our direct-to-retained-earnings method uses three entries:

  1. Dr Service revenue 4,450; Cr Retained earnings 4,450.
  2. Dr Retained earnings 2,274; Cr Wages expense 1,350, Supplies expense 600, Insurance expense 200, Depreciation expense 100 and Interest expense 24.
  3. Dr Retained earnings 400; Cr Dividends 400.

The revenue, expense and dividend accounts now have zero balances. Retained earnings has a credit balance of 1,776, because 0 + 2,176 − 400 = 1,776. Assets, liabilities, contributed capital and total equity have not changed. The post-closing trial balance totals 11,700 on each side: gross assets 11,700 versus contra asset 100, liabilities 3,824 and equity 7,776. Do not subtract accumulated depreciation twice.

Closing does not erase the journal or mean that January revenue was zero. It resets the period's temporary accumulators; the saved adjusted trial balance and entries still report January activity. Retained earnings is an equity account, not a segregated cash fund. Its 1,776 cannot be equated with the 5,300 Cash balance.

5. Settlement, reversal and correction are different operations

When the company collects a receivable or pays a payable, the original revenue or expense has already been recognized. Repeating it would double count the activity. A reversing entry is an optional bookkeeping step, typically effective at the next period's start, that swaps a selected accrual's debit and credit to simplify later routine posting. It neither forgives a debt nor revises the earlier period. Do not automatically reverse every adjustment: reversing ordinary depreciation or already consumed insurance would undo a continuing balance without justification.

Worked example 3 — Two routes to the same next-period wage expense

Harbor's January close includes Wages payable 250. On 5 February it pays 600, consisting of that 250 plus 350 earned in February. No other February activity is being modeled here.

Without reversal: Dr Wages payable 250, Dr Wages expense 350, Cr Cash 600. The payable is settled, February expense is 350 and cash falls from 5,300 to 4,700.

With reversal: effective 1 February, Dr Wages payable 250 and Cr Wages expense 250. The January close and this opening-date reversal can both be prepared on 2 February; keep the effective and recorded dates distinct. On 5 February, Dr Wages expense 600 and Cr Cash 600. February's net wage expense is 600 − 250 = 350. Wages payable ends at zero and cash at 4,700, exactly as under the first route.

Between reversal and payment, the ledger shows a credit expense and no payable for this selected item. The actual obligation has not disappeared; the linked workpaper and scheduled payment remain necessary. Reversals are a processing convention, not grounds to issue an interim report that omits an outstanding obligation. Any report before settlement must restore the appropriate accrual. Mixing the two routes—reversing first and then splitting the payment as if there had been no reversal—would understate February expense and produce a spurious debit in Wages payable.

A correcting entry instead repairs an error. Suppose a $900 collection of an existing receivable was wrongly credited to Revenue. The recorded Dr Cash 900 was right; the credit was wrong. Dr Revenue 900 and Cr Receivables 900 repairs the classification without changing cash. Keep a reference to the erroneous entry and the evidence. For our still-open reporting exercise this is a current correction; treatment of a material error in previously issued financial statements requires the applicable reporting rules, which are outside this introductory case.

6. A trial balance is a necessary check, not an audit opinion

One omitted side of an entry usually breaks equality. A wholly omitted balanced entry does not. Neither does a duplicate balanced entry, equal errors on both sides, or a balanced entry to the wrong accounts or period. For example, recording an owner's $600 contribution as Dr Cash 600 / Cr Revenue 600 balances but overstates profit by 600 and understates contributed capital by 600. Total equity still agrees with net assets.

Similarly, recording all $900 of supplies as expense when $300 remains at month end can leave the trial balance equal while understating both assets and profit by 300. Dr Supplies 300 / Cr Supplies expense 300 repairs that specific error. Never insert a mysterious expense or equity “plug” just to make two columns agree.

Check beyond arithmetic. Trace entries back to evidence for occurrence and authorization; trace source records forward for completeness. Compare customer and supplier balances with their underlying schedules. Reconcile Cash to independent bank records and outstanding items. Inspect performance dates and unpaid invoices around the reporting boundary. Count supplies, assess asset-use schedules and review unusual balances. Evidence can be incomplete or false; these procedures improve the basis for a judgment rather than guaranteeing it.

Even a correctly classified ledger does not establish that a proposed payment can occur. A forecast can balance algebraically with negative Cash. Under our no-overdraft convention that is an infeasible cash plan, not an asset the company can spend. State the required financing, its availability and timing. Profit, cash availability, book equity and market value answer different questions.

7. Reproduce the posting trail

Download the documented synthetic journal and chart, standard-library ledger program, preserved output and README. Keep them together and run python3 v07-c01-ledger.py. The default input path resolves beside the script. Output amounts are integer USD cents; divide by 100 to compare with the tables. No network, external package or random draw is used.

The program checks dated, balanced postings, records balances after each entry, builds unadjusted/adjusted/post-closing trial balances, and compares the two wage-settlement routes. It reports opposite-normal balances for investigation. It does not infer correct recognition from document labels. Deliberately replace J01's capital credit with a revenue credit: the equation still balances, but profit changes incorrectly. Then restore the source file and explain what substantive evidence catches the error. Do not confuse a passed schema check with a verified economic event.

Exercises

  1. Record and post. A separate fictional service company begins at zero. Owners contribute $1,000; it borrows $600; buys equipment for $400 cash; completes a fully collectible service on credit for $750; collects $300 of that bill; and pays an authorized $80 dividend. Use the chapter's simple conventions and ignore depreciation and interest for this exercise only. Give all six entries, the ending trial balance, profit and A = L + E. Explain why the collection and dividend do not alter revenue.
  2. Build the adjustments. At month end, another company's unadjusted Supplies balance is $480 and a count shows $125 remains. Its prepaid $600 insurance covers three equal months, one now expired. A $900 customer advance covers three distinct $300 sessions, one now completed. A different completed service worth $220 is unbilled but unconditionally collectible. Wages owed are $140; stipulated monthly depreciation is $90; and a $1,200 loan owes 1% interest for the full month. None of these seven adjustments has been recorded. Give each entry and the combined changes in profit, total assets (after depreciation) and liabilities. Check the change equation.
  3. Infer one missing balance carefully. A trial balance contains debit Cash 1,320, Receivables 480, Equipment 900, Wages expense 260 and Dividends 40; credits Trade payables 310, Loan 700, Contributed capital 1,500 and an unreadable Service revenue amount. Opening retained earnings is zero. Assume these are all accounts and exactly one unreadable figure is missing; find it, profit, closing retained earnings, assets, liabilities and equity. Give the closing entries. Explain why dropping the one-missing-figure assumption changes what can be inferred.
  4. Balanced errors. A draft month-end ledger has three independent errors: a completed $180 credit service was omitted entirely; a $250 collection of an existing receivable was credited to Revenue instead of Receivables; and six months of insurance costing $240 was wholly expensed at payment, although only one month has expired. All omitted/incorrect entries would be balanced, and no correction has yet been made. Give the correcting entries and the combined change in cash, receivables, prepaid insurance, profit and equity. Could trial-balance equality alone locate these errors?
  5. Keep the reversal route consistent. December-end wages of $180 were properly accrued and the month closed. On 5 January, $500 is paid for those wages plus $320 of January work. Show the no-reversal route and the 1 January reversal/full-payment route. A clerk instead reverses and then uses the no-reversal split: calculate January wage expense and the resulting payable balance. Explain why an interim report between reversal and payment still needs the unpaid obligation.
  6. Cost allocation is not market valuation. Equipment costing $2,400 is available on 1 July, with residual value $240 and 36 useful months. Under the stated straight-line convention find July–September expense, accumulated depreciation, net carrying amount, purchase cash outflow and equity effect from depreciation alone. If useful life had instead been stipulated as 24 months from acquisition, find the quarter's changed amounts. Under the original 36-month convention, what is carrying amount after 40 months if the equipment remains in use and there are no other changes? Does an unsolicited $2,700 price indication automatically create recorded revenue in this case?
  7. Balance versus cash feasibility. Opening balances are Cash $40, Receivables $600 and Contributed capital $640. During a short period, the company completes $800 of fully collectible services on credit, borrows $200, collects $100 of old receivables, then plans to pay $300 for equipment, $150 wages and a $40 dividend, in that order. Ignore other adjustments. Compute the proposed closing cash, profit and accounting equation. Under no overdraft, identify the smallest additional cash funding needed before the wage payment to carry out all planned payments, and record it as a new loan. Does it change profit? Distinguish a balanced proposed ledger from evidence that financing is available.
  8. Proof and evidence. Prove that a zero-sum debit-minus-credit opening ledger remains zero-sum after any sequence of balanced entries. Then refute the claim that this proves correct financial reporting with an original balanced counterexample involving either an owner payment or an unperformed service. Name four specific evidence checks addressing occurrence, completeness, period cutoff and measurement. Explain why a framework or a software account type cannot settle every actual recognition question.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Entries are: Dr Cash 1,000 / Cr Capital 1,000; Dr Cash 600 / Cr Loan 600; Dr Equipment 400 / Cr Cash 400; Dr Receivables 750 / Cr Revenue 750; Dr Cash 300 / Cr Receivables 300; Dr Dividends 80 / Cr Cash 80. Cash ends at 1,420; receivables at 450. Debit trial balances are Cash 1,420, Receivables 450, Equipment 400 and Dividends 80, totaling 2,350. Credits are Loan 600, Capital 1,000 and Revenue 750, also 2,350.

    Profit is 750. Assets are 1,420 + 450 + 400 = 2,270; liabilities 600; equity 1,000 + 750 − 80 = 1,670. Thus 2,270 = 600 + 1,670. Collection converts one asset to another; the service was already earned. The dividend distributes equity and is neither revenue nor expense.

  2. Dr Supplies expense 355 / Cr Supplies 355; Dr Insurance expense 200 / Cr Prepaid insurance 200; Dr Customer advances 300 / Cr Service revenue 300; Dr Receivables 220 / Cr Service revenue 220; Dr Wages expense 140 / Cr Wages payable 140; Dr Depreciation expense 90 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 90; Dr Interest expense 12 / Cr Interest payable 12.

    Revenue increases 520 and expenses increase 355 + 200 + 140 + 90 + 12 = 797, so profit and equity fall 277. Total assets change by −355 − 200 + 220 − 90 = −425. Liabilities change by −300 + 140 + 12 = −148. Hence −425 = −148 − 277. No entry changes cash. Booking the receivable does not require that the administrative invoice already exist, given the exercise's explicit right to payment.

  3. Debits total 1,320 + 480 + 900 + 260 + 40 = 3,000. Known credits total 310 + 700 + 1,500 = 2,510; missing revenue is 490. Profit is 490 − 260 = 230; retained earnings after closing is 230 − 40 = 190. Assets are 2,700, liabilities 1,010 and equity 1,500 + 190 = 1,690, so 2,700 = 1,010 + 1,690.

    Close with Dr Revenue 490 / Cr Retained earnings 490; Dr Retained earnings 260 / Cr Wages expense 260; Dr Retained earnings 40 / Cr Dividends 40. The post-closing debit and credit totals are each 2,700. With other missing or wrong figures, equality supplies only one constraint and cannot determine which account or amount needs correction. The calculated 490 is conditional on the stated completeness assumption.

  4. Record Dr Receivables 180 / Cr Revenue 180 for the omission. Record Dr Revenue 250 / Cr Receivables 250 to move the erroneous collection credit. Record Dr Prepaid insurance 200 / Cr Insurance expense 200 because five unexpired months remain: 240 × 5/6 = 200. Correct insurance expense is 40.

    Cash changes by zero; receivables change by 180 − 250 = −70; prepaid insurance rises 200. Revenue changes by −70, expenses by −200, so profit and equity rise 130. Assets also rise 130 and liabilities do not change. Each error and correction preserves debit-credit equality. Completion records, the customer subledger and the coverage contract/count of elapsed months supply the information that the equality lacks.

  5. Without reversal, Dr Wages payable 180, Dr Wages expense 320, Cr Cash 500. With reversal, first Dr Wages payable 180 / Cr Wages expense 180, then Dr Wages expense 500 / Cr Cash 500. Both routes give January expense 320, cash outflow 500 and zero ending payable for this item.

    The mixed route credits expense 180 at reversal but debits only 320 at payment, leaving expense 140, understated by 180. It also debits the payable twice: the opening credit 180 becomes a debit balance 180. The arithmetic still balances, but the posting no longer describes the obligation and work. Before the payment, reversal alone has not legally or economically discharged the wages; an interim report must include the still-unpaid accrual with the appropriate offset.

  6. Depreciable cost is 2,400 − 240 = 2,160. Monthly expense is 2,160/36 = 60; three months give expense and accumulated depreciation 180. Dr Depreciation expense 180 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 180. Carrying amount is 2,220. Purchase cash outflow was 2,400; depreciation itself changes cash by zero and reduces profit/equity by 180, with an equal reduction in total assets.

    At a stipulated 24-month life, monthly expense is 90, quarter expense/accumulated depreciation 270 and carrying amount 2,130. Profit/equity are 90 lower than under the 36-month convention, with no additional purchase cash outflow. Under the original convention, allocation stops at cumulative 2,160 after 36 months; at month 40 carrying amount remains 240. Continued use is possible. The $2,700 indication does not automatically produce revenue under our specified no-revaluation convention; a different reporting rule or actual disposal would need separate analysis.

  7. The proposed cash balance is 40 + 200 + 100 − 300 − 150 − 40 = −150. Profit is 800 − 150 = 650. Receivables are 600 + 800 − 100 = 1,300 and equipment 300. Algebraic assets are −150 + 1,300 + 300 = 1,450; liabilities 200; equity 640 + 650 − 40 = 1,250. The equation balances.

    After buying equipment, cash is only 40, so the wage payment already fails the no-overdraft constraint. To carry out both remaining payments requires another 150 in cash before wages: Dr Cash 150 / Cr Loan 150. Then closing cash is zero, assets 1,600, liabilities 350 and equity still 1,250. Borrowing changes no profit. The journal describes the financing if obtained; a willing lender or a changed payment plan is still needed. A negative cash forecast is not silently valid financing.

  8. Let the sum of signed opening account balances be zero. For each entry, total debit increments equal total credit increments, so its change to the signed sum is zero. By applying this observation successively, every posted prefix and the final ledger have sum zero. Equivalently, induction starts with the opening ledger and preserves the property for the next entry.

    An illustrative counterexample records a $700 advance for an entirely unperformed service as Dr Cash 700 / Cr Revenue 700. The entry balances but, under our convention, should credit Customer advances; profit and equity are overstated and liabilities understated by 700. Any distinct correct counterexample with specified rules and quantified effects earns full credit.

    Examples of four targeted checks are a customer completion confirmation for occurrence, tracing all numbered delivery records into the journal for completeness, comparing service/payroll dates around month end for cutoff, and checking useful-life/residual assumptions or remaining coverage against records for measurement. Explain which assertion each check addresses and acknowledge its limits. A software type only controls a calculation; actual recognition depends on the event, rights, obligations and applicable rules. A conceptual framework guides analysis but does not replace transaction-specific standards or evidence. Grade for the invariant proof, a valid balanced counterexample, four linked checks and clear scope, not for repeating terminology.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back: explain to a colleague how a customer receipt of $500 could increase cash without increasing revenue, how wages can reduce profit before payment, and why accumulated depreciation is a credit account without being debt. Use journal entries and finish with an accounting-equation check.

Teach-back checklist

Use either collection of an existing receivable or an advance for an unperformed service for the receipt, with its correct credit. Accrue the wages with Dr Expense / Cr Payable. Explain that the contra asset reduces equipment's net carrying amount and creates no creditor obligation or cash reserve. Debit/credit must be described as sides and tied to account type, and total debits must equal credits. State the entity, currency, period and recognition assumptions.

Delayed check, after one week: a company receives $600 on 1 March for three separately priced $200 sessions. Two are completed by 31 March. It also owes $90 for March wages. Give the initial and adjusting entries and their combined March effect on cash, profit, liabilities and equity, ignoring all other activity. If the wages are paid in April, what is the payment entry? Does a balanced trial balance prove that exactly two sessions were completed?

Delayed-check answer

Initially Dr Cash 600 / Cr Customer advances 600. At close, Dr Customer advances 400 / Cr Revenue 400 and Dr Wages expense 90 / Cr Wages payable 90. Cash rises 600; profit/equity rise 310; liabilities rise 200 + 90 = 290. Thus assets +600 = liabilities +290 + equity +310. In April, without reversal, Dr Wages payable 90 / Cr Cash 90; no April wage expense is created by this settlement. Completion evidence, not equality alone, establishes how many sessions were performed.

Sources and connection

The primary routes are MIT's accounting-process Part I, Part II on adjustments, and the IFRS Foundation's dated conceptual summary. Their inspected scope is recorded in the source catalogue. Our ledger proves consistency under supplied facts and conventions; it is not an audit of an actual business.

Next, Balance sheet, income statement and cash flow organizes account balances into linked statements and separate operating, investing and financing cash movements. Later chapters examine recognition, working capital, long-lived assets, debt, leases, tax and earnings quality. The discipline established here remains the same: preserve the event, date, counter-entry and evidence while asking what the recorded number actually means.

Sources and further study

  • S. P. Kothari — Accrual Accounting Process: Part I, MIT 15.511 (11 June 2004) — Debit and credit sides, account normal balances, temporary equity accounts, journal-to-ledger posting, trial balance and errors consistent with equal columns.
  • S. P. Kothari — Accrual Accounting Process: Part II, MIT 15.511 (14 June 2003; hosted in Summer 2004 materials) — Period-end accruals/deferrals, supplies and insurance consumption, customer advances, unpaid wages/interest, depreciation and its contra asset.
  • IFRS Foundation — Conceptual Framework Project Summary (March 2018) — Distinguish element definitions, recognition and measurement; owner movements versus income/expense; conceptual guidance versus a binding transaction-specific standard.
